key_terms.meaning: With negative feedback, an ideal op-amp forces v₊ = v₋ because its gain is infinite and the input difference must be v_o/A → 0.
If v₊ is tied to 0 V, the virtual short holds v₋ at 0 V too, even though no wire connects it to ground.
The differential gain with no feedback; ideal is infinite, a 741 has about 2×10⁵ at DC.
Small DC current into each input, pA for CMOS and about 80 nA for a 741; ideal value is zero.
v_o/v_in = −R_f/R₁; the input drives R₁ whose far end sits at virtual ground.
v_o/v_in = 1 + R_f/R₁; the signal enters v₊ and the feedback divider sets the gain.
Non-inverting case with R₁ open and R_f = 0, so gain = 1 and input resistance is very high.
Several resistors feed one virtual ground; v_o = −R_f(v₁/R₁ + v₂/R₂ + …).
v_o = (R_f/R₁)(v₂ − v₁) when R_f/R₁ = R₃/R₂; the resistor ratios must match.
20 log₁₀(A_d/A_cm) in dB; it says how well a common voltage on both inputs is ignored.
Two input buffers plus a difference stage; gain = (1 + 2R/R_G)(R_f/R₁).
Capacitor in feedback: v_o = −(1/R₁C)∫v_in dt, with time constant R₁C in seconds.
Capacitor at input, resistor in feedback: v_o = −R_fC (dv_in/dt).
Circuit that forces I_L = v_in/R into a load, independent of the load resistance.
Current-to-voltage converter: v_o = −I_in R_f, used with photodiodes and sensors.
Diode or BJT in feedback; v_o = −(kT/q) ln(v_in/I_s R), about −60 mV per decade at room temperature.
log(v₁) + log(v₂) then antilog gives v₁v₂; built from log, summing and antilog blocks.
Diode inside the feedback loop, so the 0.7 V drop is divided by A_OL and mV signals rectify.
Switch closes to charge C to v_in, then opens; C holds the value through an output buffer.
Comparator with positive feedback; two thresholds V_UT and V_LT give hysteresis and clean switching.
Two comparators with different references; output changes only when v_in leaves the band V_L to V_H.

takeaways: An ideal op-amp has infinite gain, infinite input resistance and zero output resistance, so with negative feedback the input pair becomes a virtual short that draws no current.
Two resistors and a virtual ground give every linear op-amp circuit its gain: −R_f/R₁ inverting, 1 + R_f/R₁ non-inverting, and 1 for the follower.
Sums and differences are just currents meeting at a virtual ground, which is why one op-amp can add several inputs or subtract two.
The instrumentation amplifier adds buffered inputs to a difference stage, giving very high input resistance and CMRR for measuring small signals on a large common voltage.
Swapping a resistor for a capacitor turns the same inverting stage into an integrator or a differentiator.
Feedback lets the op-amp set a voltage across a resistor, so the current through it, and through the load, is fixed by the input alone.
A diode or transistor in the feedback loop gives log and antilog responses, and combining them multiplies or divides signals.
Feedback around a diode removes its turn-on drop, and a capacitor after it holds a peak or a sample; without feedback the same op-amp becomes a comparator with two output states.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask for the circuit diagram, the derivation from the virtual-short idea, the final gain or output formula with units, and one practical limitation such as finite gain, resistor tolerance or the diode drop.

bank.q: Explain the virtual short and virtual ground concepts. Why does an ideal op-amp with negative feedback behave this way?
outline: Ideal op-amp: A_OL → ∞, R_in → ∞, R_out → 0.
Output v_o = A_OL(v₊ − v₋); with finite v_o and infinite gain the difference must be zero.
Negative feedback returns part of v_o to v₋ so the loop can settle at v₊ = v₋.
If v₊ = 0 V then v₋ sits at 0 V without being grounded: virtual ground.
Zero input current follows from infinite R_in, so the same current flows in R₁ and R_f.

bank.q: List the ideal op-amp characteristics and compare them with a practical op-amp such as the 741.
outline: Ideal: infinite gain, infinite input resistance, zero output resistance, infinite bandwidth, zero offset and drift.
Practical 741: A_OL about 2×10⁵, R_in about 2 MΩ, R_out about 75 Ω, unity-gain bandwidth about 1 MHz.
Offset voltage of a few mV, bias current of tens of nA, finite slew rate 0.5 V/µs.
Consequence: gain formula is approximate, offsets appear at the output multiplied by the closed-loop gain.
CMRR finite, typically 90 dB.

bank.q: Why is a voltage follower used as a buffer? Explain with an example of a sensor driving a heavy load.
outline: Gain = 1 because R₁ is open and R_f = 0; output follows input in phase and magnitude.
Input resistance is very high (MΩ), so it does not load a high-impedance source.
Output resistance is very low, so it can drive a low-resistance load.
Example: a divider of two 100 kΩ resistors feeding a 1 kΩ load collapses without a buffer.
Feedback keeps v₋ = v₊, so the output copies the input.

bank.q: Explain how an op-amp works as a comparator and describe its output states with ±15 V supplies.
outline: No feedback, so output is open-loop: v_o = A_OL(v₊ − v₋).
If v₊ > v₋ output swings to +V_sat, about +14 V; if v₊ < v₋ it swings to −V_sat.
Output is two-state, not linear; the transition is fast.
Reference can be 0 V or a DC level set by a divider.
Practical points: no hysteresis so noise causes chatter, limited slew rate, output must be limited for logic loads.

bank.q: Design an inverting amplifier of gain −25 using a 741 on ±15 V supplies. Choose resistors, state the input resistance, and give two guidelines for resistor selection.
outline: Gain = −R_f/R₁ = −25, so R_f = 25R₁.
Pick R₁ = 4.7 kΩ and R_f = 120 kΩ (nearest standard) or R₁ = 1 kΩ, R_f = 25 kΩ.
Input resistance seen by the source equals R₁.
Keep R₁ above about 1 kΩ so the bias-current offset stays small; keep R_f below about 1 MΩ so stray capacitance does not slow the response.
Output offset ≈ offset voltage × 25, so offset nulling may be needed.

bank.q: An inverting summer has R₁ = R₂ = R₃ = 10 kΩ and R_f = 20 kΩ. The inputs are 1 V, 2 V and −0.5 V. Find the output and the current in R_f.
outline: v_o = −R_f(v₁/R₁ + v₂/R₂ + v₃/R₃).
Each term: 0.1 mA, 0.2 mA, −0.05 mA; sum = 0.25 mA.
Virtual ground holds the summing node at 0 V, so each input current is set by its own resistor only.
Current in R_f equals the sum, 0.25 mA, flowing from the node to the output.
Check supplies: −5 V is inside ±15 V, so no clipping.

bank.q: An instrumentation amplifier uses R = 25 kΩ, R_f = 100 kΩ and R₁ = 10 kΩ. Find R_G for a total gain of 100 and explain why this circuit suits a bridge measurement.
outline: Total gain = (1 + 2R/R_G)(R_f/R₁).
Second stage gain = 100 kΩ/10 kΩ = 10, so the first stage must give 10.
Only R_G sets the gain, so one variable resistor trims the whole amplifier.
Both inputs go to non-inverting terminals, giving very high input resistance.
Mismatch in the difference stage sets CMRR; typical CMRR above 100 dB.

bank.q: An integrator has R₁ = 10 kΩ and C = 10 nF. A 1 V step is applied at t = 0. Find the output after 1 ms and sketch the response for a 1 kHz square wave.
outline: v_o = −(1/R₁C)∫v_in dt, time constant R₁C = 10 kΩ × 10 nF = 100 µs.
Slope = −v_in/(R₁C) = −1 V/100 µs = −10 V/ms.
After 1 ms, v_o = −10 V (clipped if the supply is ±15 V and the step lasts longer).
For a square wave the output is triangular; amplitude = v_in/(4fR₁C).
With 1 kHz and 1 V peak, amplitude = 1/(4 × 1000 × 100×10⁻⁶) = 2.5 V.
A resistor across C is added in practice to stop drift and set a DC limit.

bank.q: Design a voltage-to-current converter that drives 5 mA through a grounded load from a 1 V input, and show that the load value does not change the current.
outline: Use a non-inverting input at v_in with feedback that holds the same voltage across a sense resistor R.
I_L = v_in/R; for 1 V and 5 mA choose R = 200 Ω.
Virtual short keeps the sense resistor voltage equal to v_in, whatever the load is.
Explain with a floating-load version: load in the feedback path, current set by R.
For a grounded load, a Howland-type or an added buffer stage is used.
Limits: the op-amp must supply the load current, so add a transistor for currents above about 20 mA.

bank.q: Derive the output of a log amplifier using a diode in the feedback loop. Explain its temperature dependence and how an antilog stage with a summer makes an analog multiplier.
outline: Input current I = v_in/R flows through the diode because the summing node is at virtual ground.
Diode equation I = I_s(e^(v_D/V_T) − 1), so v_D = V_T ln(I/I_s) with V_T = kT/q ≈ 26 mV at 300 K.
Output v_o = −v_D = −V_T ln(v_in/(I_s R)), so it is proportional to log of the input.
Slope is about 60 mV per decade of input current at room temperature.
V_T and I_s both drift with temperature, so matched transistor pairs and temperature compensation are used.
Multiplier: log v₁ + log v₂ summed, then antilog gives v₁v₂; division subtracts the logs.

bank.q: Compare a precision half-wave rectifier with a plain diode rectifier for a 100 mV, 1 kHz sine input. Explain where the diode drop goes and what limits the precision circuit.
outline: Plain diode: output is zero until v_in exceeds about 0.7 V, so a 100 mV signal never appears.
Precision circuit: diode inside the feedback loop; the op-amp output rises until v₋ = v₊, so the drop is supplied by the op-amp, not taken from the signal.
Effective error is about 0.7 V/A_OL, i.e. microvolts.
Limits: op-amp slew rate and gain-bandwidth at high frequency; the op-amp must come out of saturation quickly when the input reverses.
Use a second diode or a resistor to keep the loop closed near zero crossing and avoid dead time.
Full-wave version uses two diodes and a summing stage.

bank.q: Design a Schmitt trigger with thresholds at +2 V and −2 V using ±12 V supplies. Derive the threshold expressions and explain why hysteresis rejects noise.
outline: Positive feedback from output to v₊ through R₂, input through R₁; output is at ±V_sat.
Upper threshold V_UT = +V_sat·R₁/(R₁+R₂) + V_ref·R₂/(R₁+R₂) when output is high.
Lower threshold V_LT with −V_sat in the same expression.
Choose R₁/R₂ from V_UT = 2 V with V_sat ≈ 11 V; a reference shifts the band if needed.
Hysteresis width V_UT − V_LT keeps noise smaller than the band from causing extra output changes.
Uses: squaring up slow waves, zero-crossing detectors, removing contact bounce.

bank.q: Compare the inverting and non-inverting configurations for input resistance, gain accuracy, common-mode voltage at the input and bandwidth. Which one would you pick to buffer a high-impedance sensor?
outline: Inverting: input resistance = R₁, gain −R_f/R₁, inputs stay at virtual ground so no common-mode voltage, but low input resistance loads the source.
Non-inverting: input resistance very high (set by the op-amp), gain 1 + R_f/R₁, both inputs move with the signal so CMRR and input capacitance matter.
Noise gain is 1 + R_f/R₁ in both cases, so closed-loop bandwidth = f_T/(1 + R_f/R₁).
Gain error comes from finite A_OL and resistor tolerance; the non-inverting form gives a slightly lower gain than calculated.
For a high-impedance sensor use the non-inverting form or a follower first, then an inverting stage for gain.
Both are limited by offset voltage times the DC gain at the output.

bank.q: Explain how feedback around a diode and a capacitor produces a peak detector and a sample-and-hold. Include the role of the switch, the hold capacitor and the droop.
outline: Precision peak detector: diode in the feedback loop charges C to the input peak; the op-amp compensates the diode drop.
When the input falls, the diode blocks unless a reset switch or resistor is added.
Droop: C discharges through leakage and bias current, so v falls at I/C; a larger C and a FET-input op-amp reduce it.
Sample-and-hold: an analog switch connects v_in to C during the sample interval; the buffer holds the value when the switch opens.
Acquisition time is set by the switch resistance and C; aperture time is the switching delay.
Used in ADCs, DMMs and peak-reading meters; the buffer after C must have very high input resistance.

glossary.def: A high-gain differential amplifier in one package, usually with two inputs and one output.
The near-zero voltage difference between the two inputs of an op-amp working with negative feedback.
A node held at 0 V by feedback even though it is not connected to ground.
The gain of the op-amp with no feedback path, very large at DC and falling with frequency.
The fastest rate at which the output can change, in V/µs.
The frequency at which open-loop gain falls to 1, equal to closed-loop gain times closed-loop bandwidth.
The small differential voltage needed at the input to make the output exactly zero.
The small DC current that flows into each input terminal.
The ratio of differential gain to common-mode gain, usually quoted in dB.
An op-amp stage whose gain is −R_f/R₁ and whose output is 180° out of phase with the input.
An op-amp stage whose gain is 1 + R_f/R₁ with the output in phase with the input.
A gain-of-one buffer made from an op-amp with the output tied to the inverting input.
A circuit that adds several input voltages, each scaled by its own resistor.
A circuit that amplifies the voltage difference between two inputs and rejects the common part.
A three-op-amp circuit with very high input resistance and CMRR, used for sensor and bridge signals.
A circuit whose output is proportional to the time integral of the input, made with a capacitor in feedback.
A circuit whose output is proportional to the rate of change of the input.
Ratio of output current to input voltage, the quantity a V-I converter sets.
Ratio of output voltage to input current, set by R_f in a current-to-voltage converter.
A circuit using the exponential diode or transistor characteristic to give an output proportional to log of the input.
A rectifier with the diode inside the op-amp feedback loop, so it works down to millivolts.
A diode and capacitor circuit that stores the highest input voltage reached.
A circuit that tracks the input and then freezes it on a capacitor when a switch opens.
The gap between the upper and lower threshold voltages that stops a comparator from chattering on noise.
A pair of comparators that flags when an input lies outside an allowed voltage band.
